title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is correcting the lunar tables (node and inclination) from the observed contact times of a lunar eclipse.

Setup and notation.
- ☊ is the ascending node. σ and λ are the shadow centre and the moon's centre at mid-eclipse, with ☊σ = x.
- m, n, k are hourly motions in arc seconds. The relative motion n−m is reduced by the factor g. The small longitude correction is c = (m+n+2k) sin2x tan²(ρ/2) / [g(n−m)].
- On the previous page Euler used the first and last outer contacts. These are separated by h hours, and at each the separation of centres is SL = sl = f, the sum of the shadow and moon radii.
- Writing a = ½h(n+k) and b = ½h(m+k), the spherical triangle S☊L has sides x−a−c and x−b and angle ρ. This gives cos f = cosρ sin(x−a−c) sin(x−b) + cos(x−a−c) cos(x−b).
- Putting cosρ = 1 − 2sin²(ρ/2) and using product-to-sum identities gives
  sin²(ρ/2)·cos(2x−a−b−c) = cos f − cos²(ρ/2)·cos(a−b+c).

§18. That page had obtained tan(2x−c) from the first and last contacts alone. Euler now judges this too sensitive to small errors in c. In a total eclipse he therefore adds the inner contacts (immersion and emersion).
- At these SL = F = α−β, the difference of the two radii.
- They are separated by H hours. Put A = ½H(n+k) and B = ½H(m+k).
- By the same argument: sin²(ρ/2)·cos(2x−A−B−c) = cos F − cos²(ρ/2)·cos(A−B+c).

§19. Dividing the two relations removes sin²(ρ/2). Euler argues that cos²(ρ/2) ≈ 1 is insensitive to errors in ρ and that its errors roughly cancel between numerator and denominator.
- Expand cos(2x−u) = cos2x(cos u + sin u·tan2x) and call the right-hand ratio d.
- This gives the linear relation cos(a+b+c) + sin(a+b+c)·tan2x = d·[cos(A+B+c) + sin(A+B+c)·tan2x].
- Hence tan2x = [d·cos(A+B+c) − cos(a+b+c)] / [sin(a+b+c) − d·sin(A+B+c)].
- This gives the node distance ☊σ = x.

§20. With x known, the inclination ρ is refined from equivalent forms:
- sin²(ρ/2) = [cos f − cos²(ρ/2)·cos(a−b+c)] / cos(2x−a−b−c), solved iteratively;
- cosρ = [cos f − cos(x−a−c)·cos(x−b)] / [sin(x−a−c)·sin(x−b)];
- sin²(ρ/2) = [cos(a−b+c) − cos f] / [2 sin(x−a−c)·sin(x−b)];
- sin²(ρ/2) = [cos(a−b+c) − cos f] / [cos(a−b+c) − cos(2x−a−b−c)];
- sin²(ρ/2) = sin((f+a−b+c)/2)·sin((f−a+b−c)/2) / [sin(x−a−c)·sin(x−b)].

Purpose: to correct the tables of the lunar node and inclination using eclipse timings.
errors: All the algebra on the page checks out. Verified: the passage from the cosine rule to the cos(2x−a−b−c) form, the quotient, the tan2x formula, and all the alternative expressions for sin²(ρ/2) and cosρ.
The method assumes the same small correction c for both pairs of contacts and uniform motions over the eclipse. This is acceptable to the order Euler works at.

Unremarked conditioning problem (beyond the cancellation argument Euler does make). In planar terms each pair of contacts gives a chord: (half-duration × relative speed)² + q² = (contact distance)², where q is the least separation of centres. The two chords therefore fix q and the relative speed v.
q ≈ ρ sin x, while v² ≈ (n−m)² + nm(ρ cos x)². So the information on x enters only through a relative change in v of order nmρ²/(n−m)² ≈ 10⁻³.

Extracting x would therefore require contact times good to a few seconds. Penumbral fuzziness makes this impossible in practice, and d is close to 1 so the tan2x denominator is a difference of nearly equal quantities.
Euler's claim that errors in cos²(ρ/2) compensate is therefore true but not the real issue. He himself warns on the next page that such formulas 'nimium a veritate seducant', without quantifying why.

ideas.what: Determining the lunar node distance and inclination from the timings of eclipse contacts, via spherical triangles at the node
ideas.modern_name: Reduction of lunar eclipse observations to correct the orbital elements (node, inclination)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ancient practice (Hipparchus/Ptolemy used eclipses for lunar elements); 18th-century refinements by Euler, Mayer, Lalande and others
ideas.where_published: This posthumous piece (E838, Opera postuma 1862); related material in Euler's lunar theories (E187, E418) is possible but unconfirmed

ideas.what: Using the inner contacts of a total eclipse together with the outer contacts, and taking quotients of the two relations to eliminate sin²(ρ/2)
ideas.modern_name: Elimination of a nuisance parameter between two observation equations
ideas.where_published: E838 only, as far as known

ideas.what: Product-to-sum rewritings of the side–angle–side cosine rule in half-angle form
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical spherical trigonometry (Euler systematised it in E214 and related works)

missed.claim: The page implicitly contains a conditioning problem that Euler senses but does not analyse. With the moon's motions taken from tables, the node distance enters the four-contact data only through a second-order (ρ²) effect on the relative speed. Euler's 'complete' solution (§19–21) is therefore numerically worthless, a point he only hints at.
missed.quote: Etsi autem in ea etiamnunc terminus cos²½ρ ... errores hinc oriundi in numeratore et denominatore fere se mutuo compensabunt
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical interest: an early example of an 18th-century astronomer confronting an ill-posed inversion. It is not a new mathematical result.

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine spherical-trigonometric reduction of eclipse observations, and it is correct. The only point of interest is Euler's informal awareness of error sensitivity; nothing here appears to be a missed result.
transcription_corrections: The line truncated at the right margin should read 'Quodsi ergo ponatur ½H(n+k) = A, ½H(m+k) = B', consistent with the later use of A and B.
'erit f ...' is cut off at the margin; by context it reads f = α+β (outer contact), while F = α−β (inner contact).
In §19 the image reads 'fere se mutuo compensabunt'.
In §20 the last numerator factor is sin((f−a+b−c)/2) and the denominator is sin(x−a−c)·sin(x−b); the image is partly cut off at the right margin.
'a veritate discrepet' is split across lines as 'a veri-tate'.
